In this question, I feel stat /etc/ssh/sshd_config is a correct answer too as shown in the screenshot below. In the screenshot, I’ve shown the date(time), followed by stat on a file, followed by editing that file, followed by stat to show the difference in Access/Modify/Change times of the file.

And following this by editing the file again but without making any changes and quiting and then doing stat again to show that Modify/Change don’t change compared to the previous stat but only access time changes.

This gives enough information to know the file has been tampered with which is what the question is asking - Which of the following commands can help her detect any tampering of the current sshd_config file?

posts.name: Sayan Ghosh
posts.cooked: It is not possible with stat alone to find out if the file has been tampered with, unless you memorize the timestamp of your last authorized modification. You need to compare the backup and the original to do so, this can be done using commands like cmp, diff, diff on the sha256sum, or directly using sha256sum -c.

posts.name: Rajagopalan Vaidyanathan
posts.cooked:
Hi,

Thanks for getting back on this.

The very fact that stat shows mtime, atime and ctime is enough to know it’s been modified, I don’t have to check anything else to know it has been tampered with. That’s what the question is asking.

What’s modified etc. are irrelevant to know if it is modified, isn’t it? The question is “Which of the following commands can help her detect any tampering of the current sshd_config file” and stat certainly gives that information.

I’m not sure why I need to memorize the timestamp because if it is tampered, it will be recent(closer to when I’m looking at it). Some time in the past and recent time certainly will tell you if it is changed recently.

Regards

Rajagopalan Vaidyanathan

posts.name: Sayan Ghosh
posts.cooked:
You do not need to know what is changed, but you do need to know if it has been changed. How will you know if it is tampered with if the mtime is way in the past as well? If it was tampered long back? Only way to definitively know the file has been tampered with is if you know the correct (last authorized edit) mtime.

This logic does not hold, hence there is no changes to this question.

posts.name: Rajagopalan Vaidyanathan
posts.cooked:
Well, if you go down that path, then I have to argue that the backup file may also have been tampered with to bring it in line with the current config file.

Any smart person who knows what he/she is doing will certainly leave nothing to chance! So, the option to use backup file as bulletproof is also stretching it like you’ve mentioned - what if it was changed long back.

posts.name: Sayan Ghosh
posts.cooked:
1. Yes, anything is possible, but that is not what the question asks, it clearly states that only the original file has been suspected of tampering, not the backup.
  2. Most times backups are kept on a separate server / offline to prevent this, and can later be copied back when checking, so it is less likely that both the files are tampered with.
  3. Your method of checking the mtime does not provide any way of finding if the last change (mtime) was authorized or unauthorized.

Only way to know is to have some note-keeping of the last authorized edit – either the entire file (sshd_config.bak), the checksum of the file (original_hash.txt), or the exact mtime (which is not part of the options), otherwise, you cannot acertain if the file is tampered with or not.

posts.name: Rajagopalan Vaidyanathan
posts.cooked:
@sayan,

The given commands - diff, CMP and sha256 - in the question doesn’t show the backup file in a different server - so it has to be on the same server. This is as per the question and given answer options. So you cannot bring up all those things for your argument. I can answer only based on what’s given in the question and it doesn’t say it’s on a different server, not the commands for diff and CMP say that when comparing them.

You have to be fair in looking at what’s asked, what’s given and ask yourself if what you are saying makes sense relative to that.

Regards

Rajagopalan Vaidyanathan

posts.name: Sayan Ghosh
posts.cooked:
It is not part of the question, we do not expect you to assume it. Similarly, we also do not expect you to assume extra things not mentioned in the question like the backup file being tampered with.

This was my explanation to your misconceptions, not clarifying or adding to the original question.

Please follow the question as it is given, it was a pretty simple question of how to compare if a file (and only that file) is suspected of being modified by using a genuine copy. The arguments presented in your replies do not hold, as have been explained in my previous replies. A file’s mtime is not indicative of whether the last edit was authorized or not. I will not go into the same explanation again and again. I can understand that you have marked one of the incorrect options and want to rationalize it to be correct, however, as stated, there is no change in this question or option evaluation to be considered.

And, talking about rationalizing, I still do remember your argument about copying and interleaved being the same - that’s rationalizing!
